title: Introduction to medical chemistry. Chemistry and the environment. Chemistry of biogenic elements

goals.text: To teach the student the tasks of medical chemistry and the stages of studying it, the mathematical skills needed for chemical calculations, chemical pollution of the environment and its effect on health, the rules of work in a chemical laboratory, and the properties, biological significance and qualitative reactions of s-, p- and d-elements.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the subject and tasks of medical chemistry and its links with other medical sciences;
the concepts of the mole, molar mass, mass fraction and concentration;
the main chemical pollutants of the environment and their effects on the body;
the classification of biogenic elements (macro-, micro- and ultramicroelements);
the physical and chemical properties and biological significance of s-, p- and d-elements;
the qualitative reactions of important cations and anions.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: follow the safety rules of a chemical laboratory and give first aid;
do simple calculations with moles, mass and concentration;
identify ions of biogenic elements with qualitative reactions;
solve situational problems and explain the chemical basis of an element deficiency or excess.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: About 97 % of body mass is made up of the **organogenic** elements — C, H, O, N, P, S. Macroelements make up more than 10^−2^ % of the body, microelements 10^−3^–10^−5^ %, and ultramicroelements less than 10^−5^ %.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Flame colors: **“Sodium — a yellow sun, Potassium — a violet night, Calcium — a brick wall, Copper — a green leaf”**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: When diluting an acid, pour the **acid into the water**, never the reverse: if water is poured into concentrated H~2~SO~4~, the heat released boils the water instantly and the acid spatters.

sections.title: 1. The subject of medical chemistry and how to study it

blocks.text: **Medical chemistry** is the science that studies the laws of the chemical and physicochemical processes in a living organism, the properties of the substances that enter the body (food, drugs, poisons) and the methods used to analyze them. It brings together the parts of general, inorganic, physical and colloid, analytical and bioorganic chemistry that medicine needs, and it is the foundation for **biochemistry, normal physiology, pharmacology, hygiene and clinical laboratory diagnostics**.

For example, to understand the acid–base status of the blood (pH 7.35–7.45) one needs buffer systems; to understand water–electrolyte metabolism one needs solutions and osmosis; to understand how drugs act one needs the structure of organic compounds.

items: **Theory** — learn terms, definitions and laws by understanding their logic, not by rote.
**Formulas and equations** — write and balance reaction equations correctly.
**Calculation** — consolidate knowledge quantitatively by solving problems.
**Experiment** — check the theory with your own eyes in laboratory work.
**Medical interpretation** — link the result to the state of the body.

blocks.text: The calculations use **decimal logarithms** (pH, pK), **powers of ten** (10^−7^ mol/L), **proportions** and **unit conversions** (mL → L, mg → g, mmol → mol) most often. Checking the units at the end of every calculation prevents half of all mistakes.

parts.text: 1 mole of any substance contains 6.022·10^23^ particles. At standard conditions (0 °C, 101.3 kPa) 1 mole of a gas occupies 22.4 L.

blocks.text: The human body constantly exchanges matter with the environment: any chemical that enters with air, water or food eventually reaches the tissues. Substances released into the environment in amounts far above the natural cycle and harmful to living organisms are called **ecotoxicants**.

blocks.text: **Global problems:** the rise of CO~2~ and CH~4~ — the greenhouse effect; chlorofluorocarbons (freons) — destruction of the ozone layer and stronger ultraviolet radiation; the reaction of SO~2~ and NO~x~ with water — **acid rain** (pH < 5.6).

parts.text: The **Aral Sea disaster** is a vivid example of a regional ecological problem. Dust made of salt and pesticide residues blown from the dried seabed has increased respiratory diseases, anemia, and kidney and liver diseases in Karakalpakstan and Khorezm. The high mineral content of drinking water promotes kidney stone formation.

sections.title: 3. Rules of work in a chemical laboratory

items: Work in the laboratory only in a lab coat; wear safety goggles and gloves when needed.
Eating, drinking and tasting reagents at the workplace are strictly forbidden.
Smell a substance without bending over the vessel: waft the air toward yourself with your hand.
When heating a test tube, never point its mouth at yourself or at a neighbor.
Work with volatile, toxic and odorous substances only in a **fume hood**.
When diluting concentrated acids, pour the **acid in a thin stream into the water**.
Draw a solution into a pipette with a **rubber bulb** (pipette filler), never by mouth.
Do not use flammable liquids (ether, alcohol, acetone) near an open flame.
After work, return the reagents to their places, clean the workplace and wash your hands.

parts.text: It is a mistake to “neutralize” acid on the skin immediately with an alkali: the heat of the neutralization reaction deepens the burn. First **plenty of water**, then a weak neutralizing solution.

blocks.text: Elements that are part of the body and perform a definite function in vital processes are called **biogenic elements**. V.I. Vernadsky showed that the elemental composition of the body reflects that of the Earth’s crust, yet living organisms accumulate some elements (C, N, P, I) thousands of times more than their surroundings.

blocks.text: Most of the body mass is made up of **oxygen (≈ 62 %)**, **carbon (≈ 21 %)**, **hydrogen (≈ 10 %)**, **nitrogen (≈ 3 %)**, **calcium (≈ 2 %)** and **phosphorus (≈ 1 %)**.

blocks.label: Figure 1.1
blocks.caption: Position of the biogenic elements in the periodic table: macroelements, microelements and organogenic elements are highlighted (drawn on the basis of D.I. Mendeleev’s periodic table).

blocks.text: The biological role of an element is linked to its **position in the periodic table**: s-elements act mainly as ions (Na^+^, K^+^, Ca^2+^, Mg^2+^) in electrolyte and structural roles; p-elements form the skeleton of biomolecules; d-elements, thanks to their variable valence and ability to form complexes, sit in the active center of **metalloenzymes**.

parts.text: One and the same element can be both essential and toxic: it all depends on the **dose**. For example, fluoride strengthens tooth enamel in small doses but causes **fluorosis** in excess; selenium deficiency causes cardiomyopathy, its excess causes selenosis.

blocks.text: s-Elements are the elements in which the s-orbital of the outer electron shell is being filled: **group IA** (Li, Na, K) — the alkali metals, and **group IIA** (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) — the alkaline earth metals. They are **soft, light, reactive metals**; they give up electrons easily and form stable ions with oxidation states +1 and +2.

**Chemical properties:** they react vigorously with water to form an alkali: 2Na + 2H~2~O → 2NaOH + H~2~↑. Metallic character and reactivity increase down a group (K is more reactive than Na). Their oxides and hydroxides are basic; Ca and Mg salts (carbonates, phosphates) are poorly soluble in water — this is the chemical basis of bone and stone formation.

parts.text: **Hyperkalemia** (K^+^ > 5.5 mmol/L) disturbs cardiac conduction and may lead to asystole; **hypokalemia** causes muscle weakness and arrhythmia. **Hypocalcemia** raises neuromuscular excitability and causes **tetany** (spasms). Lithium salts (Li~2~CO~3~) are used to treat bipolar disorder.

blocks.text: p-Elements are the elements of groups IIIA–VIIIA; p-orbitals are being filled in their outer shell. Non-metallic character increases from left to right across a period: B and Al are amphoteric, C, N, O, S and P are non-metals, and F, Cl, Br and I are the halogens (the most reactive non-metals). Most of them have variable oxidation states (nitrogen from −3 to +5) and form covalent bonds.

parts.text: Uzbekistan is an **iodine-deficiency endemic region**. Iodine deficiency enlarges the thyroid gland (endemic goiter), and deficiency during pregnancy causes cretinism in the child. This is why table salt is iodized (KIO~3~ is added).

blocks.text: **Dose-dependent effect of fluoride:** about 1 mg/L of fluoride in drinking water prevents caries, because F^−^ replaces OH^−^ in hydroxyapatite Ca~10~(PO~4~)~6~(OH)~2~ and forms acid-resistant **fluorapatite** Ca~10~(PO~4~)~6~F~2~. More than 1.5 mg/L causes spots on the enamel (fluorosis).

d-Elements (transition metals) are the elements in which the d-orbital of the next-to-outer shell is being filled (groups IB–VIIIB). Their common properties are **variable oxidation states** (Fe^2+^/Fe^3+^, Cu^+^/Cu^2+^), the **formation of complex compounds** and **colored** compounds. These very features make them an essential part of oxidation–reduction enzymes.

parts.text: In hemoglobin, iron binds O~2~ in the **Fe^2+^** state. Hemoglobin oxidized to Fe^3+^ — **methemoglobin** — cannot carry oxygen. Nitrites and some drugs (dapsone, local anesthetics) cause methemoglobinemia; it is treated with methylene blue.
To remember the metalloenzymes: **“Iron — respiration, Copper — oxidase, Zinc — carbonic anhydrase, Cobalt — B~12~, Molybdenum — xanthine”**.

blocks.text: A **qualitative reaction** is a reaction that allows an ion to be identified by a clear external sign (a precipitate, a color, a gas, a flame color). The reaction must be **sensitive** (detect even small amounts) and **selective** (specific).

parts.text: Calcium oxalate precipitates not only in the test tube but also in the body: when urine contains much Ca^2+^ and oxalate, **oxalate stones** form in the kidney — about 70–80 % of all kidney stones are of this type.

sections.title: 9. Nuclear chemistry and its significance in medicine (independent work)

blocks.text: **Radioactivity** is the spontaneous emission of radiation by unstable atomic nuclei, which turn into other nuclei. Atoms of the same element with different mass numbers are called **isotopes** (for example, ^12^C, ^13^C, ^14^C); radioactive isotopes are called **radionuclides**.

items: **α-decay** — a helium nucleus (^4^He) leaves the nucleus; the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2; it travels only a few micrometers in tissue.
**β^−^-decay** — a neutron turns into a proton and an electron is emitted; the atomic number rises by 1.
**β^+^-decay** — a proton turns into a neutron and a positron is emitted; the positron annihilates with an electron, giving two γ-quanta (the basis of PET).
**γ-radiation** — a high-energy electromagnetic wave; it has the greatest penetrating power.

blocks.text: **Law of radioactive decay:** N = N~0~·e^−λt^, where λ = ln2 / T~½~. The **half-life** (T~½~) is the time in which half of the radionuclide atoms decay. The unit of activity is the **becquerel** (1 Bq = 1 decay/s); absorbed dose is measured in **grays** (Gy), equivalent dose in **sieverts** (Sv).

parts.text: For diagnostics, **short-lived**, mainly **γ-emitting** radionuclides (^99m^Tc) are chosen, so the patient receives little radiation. For treatment, **β-emitters** that destroy tissue (^131^I) are used.

skills.title: Skill: identifying cations and anions with qualitative reactions

items: Pour 1–2 mL of the test solution into a clean test tube.
Add the reagent dropwise (3–5 drops) and mix.
Record the observed sign (color of the precipitate, color change, gas).
Check the solubility of the precipitate (for example, add ammonia to AgCl or acetic acid to CaC~2~O~4~).
Write the reaction equation in molecular and ionic form.
Conclusion: state which ion is present in the solution.

skills.title: Skill: identifying a metal ion by its flame color

items: Dip a nichrome (or platinum) wire into concentrated HCl and heat it in the flame until it no longer colors the flame.
Dip the wire into the test salt solution.
Place the wire in the colorless part of the burner flame.
Observe the flame color; for potassium, look through blue cobalt glass (it blocks the yellow color of sodium).
Clean the wire again with HCl after each sample.

cases.title: Problem 1
cases.text: A patient is receiving a 0.9 % sodium chloride solution (normal saline). Take the density of the solution as 1 g/mL (M(NaCl) = 58.5 g/mol).
cases.ask: How many grams of NaCl are in 500 mL of the solution? What is its molar concentration?
cases.answer: The mass of 500 mL of solution is 500 g; m(NaCl) = 500 · 0.009 = 4.5 g. n(NaCl) = 4.5 / 58.5 = 0.077 mol; C = 0.077 / 0.5 = 0.154 mol/L (≈ 154 mmol/L). Each NaCl gives two ions, so the osmolarity is ≈ 308 mOsm/L — close to blood plasma (isotonic).

cases.title: Problem 2
cases.text: A one-year-old child was fed formula prepared with well water. The child’s lips and nails are blue, and the cyanosis does not decrease when oxygen is given. The blood is brownish.
cases.ask: What condition is suspected? What is its chemical basis, and how is it treated?
cases.answer: Nitrate (methemoglobin) poisoning. Nitrates in the well water are reduced to nitrite in the intestine; nitrite oxidizes the Fe^2+^ of hemoglobin to Fe^3+^ — methemoglobin cannot bind O~2~, so giving oxygen does not help. Treatment: methylene blue (it returns Fe^3+^ to Fe^2+^ via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase), ascorbic acid; change the water source.

cases.title: Problem 3
cases.text: A patient with thyroid cancer received ^131^I with an activity of 3700 MBq (T~½~ = 8 days).
cases.ask: What activity remains in the body after 24 days (ignore physiological excretion)? Why is ^131^I chosen?
cases.answer: 24 days = 3 half-lives: A = 3700 · (1/2)^3^ = 3700 / 8 = 462.5 MBq. Iodine is actively taken up only by thyroid cells; the β-particles of ^131^I travel a few millimeters in tissue and destroy precisely the gland (tumor) cells, while its γ-radiation allows the process to be followed by scintigraphy.
